proposal: The Mandate criticizes Executive Order 14086, which implements the EU-US Data Privacy Framework by aligning US signals intelligence practices with European privacy standards, as a possible burden on intelligence collection. It recommends that an incoming President order an immediate study of how the order is being implemented, suspend provisions that unduly burden collection, and tell European governments that continued intelligence sharing depends on resolving the data-transfer issue within the first two years of the term.

status_summary: No presidential order, memorandum or study revoking, suspending, amending or reviewing Executive Order 14086 was found as of 2026-10-18; Federal Register queries returned only Commerce information-collection notices of 2026-02-23 and 2026-06-01 that continue the Data Privacy Framework, and the Berkeley Technology Law Journal (2026-02-26) reports no action to revoke or alter the order. The order's machinery has continued to operate: PCLOB reported on 2025-09-25 that intelligence community elements had updated their policies to comply, and said on 2025-11-13 that the redress mechanism had one qualifying complaint pending. Related events are not the step the Mandate describes: three Democratic PCLOB members were removed on 2025-01-22 (a district court's reinstatement of two was stayed by the D.C. Circuit on 2025-07-01, and that court, which had held the appeal in abeyance from 2025-10-01 pending Trump v. Slaughter, returned it to its active docket on 2026-08-05 and by clerk's order of 2026-09-18 set oral argument for 2026-11-17, before Judges Henderson, Pillard and Edwards per its calendar), and CRS reports that FISA Section 702 lapsed under its sunset on 2026-06-12 with collection continuing under existing certifications. No public US message to European governments tying intelligence sharing to the data-transfer issue was found, and in the EU the General Court dismissed the Latombe challenge on 2025-09-03, which Latombe appealed on 2025-10-31.

timeline.event: President Trump removes three Democratic members of the PCLOB, the body that reviews the redress mechanism under EO 14086 and recommends judges for the Data Protection Review Court; Beth Williams, a Republican, remains. Commentators cited by Just Security say the removals raise European doubts about the board's independence.

The D.C. Circuit (Katsas, Rao, Walker) stays pending appeal the district court's order of 2025-05-21, which had declared the removals of members LeBlanc and Felten null and void and returned them to the board, in LeBlanc v. PCLOB (No. 25-5197).
The EU General Court dismisses Philippe Latombe's action to annul the Commission's adequacy decision for the Data Privacy Framework (T-553/23), so the framework stands subject to appeal.

PCLOB releases a staff report on how intelligence community elements implemented EO 14086, finding that they updated policies, procedures and training, handle non-US persons' signals intelligence data in line with US persons' rules, and had reported no significant non-compliance incident; Board Member Williams endorses it. This is a review by an oversight board, not a presidential study or suspension.

By per curiam order (Pillard, Walker and Ginsburg; USCA Document #2138144, per the docket), the D.C. Circuit removed LeBlanc v. PCLOB (No. 25-5197) from the 2025-10-28 oral argument calendar and held it in abeyance pending the Supreme Court's decision in Trump v. Slaughter, No. 25-332, directing the parties to file motions to govern future proceedings within 30 days of that disposition; the docket also records that an en banc petition against the 2025-07-01 stay, construed as a motion for en banc reconsideration, was denied on 2025-07-18.
Latombe appeals the General Court judgment to the Court of Justice, asking it to set the judgment aside and annul the adequacy decision.

PCLOB states that the EO 14086 redress mechanism, operational since 2023-07-10, has received one qualifying complaint that the ODNI Civil Liberties Protection Officer is adjudicating, so the board cannot yet review or certify the mechanism.

The Berkeley Technology Law Journal describes the Data Privacy Framework as in force but contested, reports no administration action to revoke or alter EO 14086, and notes that safeguards resting on executive orders can be changed by any later administration.

Commerce's International Trade Administration publishes a notice submitting the Data Privacy Framework self-certification information collection to OMB, citing EO 14086 as a basis (a similar notice appeared 2026-02-23, and one on arbitrator lists on 2026-06-02), indicating the program was still being administered.

A CEPA analysis says that, after the Supreme Court's 2026-06-29 decision in Trump v. Slaughter permitting removal of FTC commissioners, the framework's assumption of independent supervision is hard to sustain; it reports that the Commission must decide in 2027 whether its 2023 finding remains justified and that FISA Section 702 was not renewed by its June 2026 deadline, with surveillance continuing under existing certifications.

The D.C. Circuit (Katsas, Rao, Childs; per curiam), on a joint motion to govern future proceedings and an unopposed motion to expedite oral argument, returned LeBlanc v. PCLOB (No. 25-5197) to its active docket, set supplemental briefs for both sides for 2026-08-21 (up to 4,000 words) and response briefs for 2026-09-11 (up to 2,000 words), and directed the Clerk to calendar oral argument on the first appropriate date after briefing; the order sets no argument date and names no Supreme Court decision (read in a RECAP copy of the filed order, which matches the copy hosted by Wolters Kluwer CCH).
